MASSIVE AIR DEFENSE BOOST: The U.S. has approved a potential $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 MSE missiles to Ukraine, fully funded by European allies.

In one of the largest air defense authorizations of the war, the U.S. State Department cleared a major Foreign Military Sale to provide Ukraine with 500 advanced Patriot interceptors, according to reporting from Reuters and Army Recognition.

The breakdown of the deal:

500 Lockheed Martin PAC-3 MSE (Missile Segment Enhancement) missiles—the most advanced hit-to-kill kinetic interceptors in Western arsenals, engineered specifically to destroy high-speed Russian ballistic threats including Iskander-M and Kinzhal missiles.

 The entire $2.1 billion tab is being financed by European allies (including Germany, the Netherlands, and Norway) and Canada, requiring zero U.S. taxpayer appropriations.

 While the contract greenlights critical long-term replenishments, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged allies to supply interceptors directly from existing active stockpiles immediately, warning that production lead times cannot leave cities unprotected through the upcoming winter heating season.

With Russian winter strike campaigns targeting power grids and urban centers, securing scarce Patriot interceptors remains the most contested logistical fight in modern air defense.

Can Western production lines scale fast enough to meet global demand for Patriot missiles, or are allied stockpiles running on empty?

Sean Strickland Opens Up On Surviving Domestic Abuse And Finding Refuge In The Octagon
Shawn Ryan Show Appearance Former UFC Middleweight Champion Sean Strickland joined The Shawn Ryan Show Episode 325 for an extensive interview detailing his childhood trauma, overcoming severe domestic violence, and how mixed martial arts channeled his anger

In Sean Strickland’s Own Words

“People look at me and think I’m just crazy or reckless, but they have no idea what home was like growing up. My dad was an abusive alcoholic filled with pure hatred. I remember nights hiding under my bed listening to him beat my mom, hearing screaming and shattering glass. One night he walked into the room with a loaded shotgun, racked it, and held it right against my mother’s forehead while I was standing there watching. I grew up filled with so much violent rage that I couldn't function in society. I was kicked out of school, had no diploma, no car, no money. At 17, I was riding a bicycle to an MMA gym and sleeping on the sweat-stained mats at night because I had nowhere else to go. I hated myself. I felt like a worthless piece of shit. The cage was the only place in the entire world where violence was acceptable, where all that darkness inside me could actually keep me alive.”

“DARK SKIES. NO FEAR. WHEN DARKNESS FALLS, THE F-35 RISES.”

While adversaries rely on darkness for cover, 5th-generation stealth fighters turn the night into their primary hunting ground.

Parked on the deck of an amphibious assault ship with glowing green formation lights cutting through the storm, the F-35 Lightning II represents the pinnacle of modern all-weather air power:

• Seeing Through the Cockpit: Through its Distributed Aperture System (DAS)—a network of six high-resolution infrared cameras embedded around the fuselage—the F-35 projects a seamless 360-degree thermal night-vision image directly onto the pilot’s Gen III helmet-mounted visor, allowing aviators to literally "look through" the floor and airframe into pitch-black airspace.

• Undetected in Contested Skies: Radar-absorbent materials, internal weapons bays, and low-probability-of-intercept (LPI) AN/APG-81 AESA radar give pilots first-look, first-shot lethality against hostile surface-to-air missile batteries and airborne threats before the enemy even knows they’re on radar.

• Expeditionary Sea Basing: This short takeoff and vertical landing (STOVL) F-35B variant operates directly from naval flat-tops and austere expeditionary airfields worldwide, bringing stealth strike capability to remote combat theaters without requiring 10,000-foot commercial runways.

With helmet-integrated sensor fusion that turns midnight into daylight, is the F-35 the most lethal night-fighting platform in modern aviation history?

“HE HAD A FRACTION OF A SECOND TO SAVE HIS MEN. HE CHOSE TO SACRIFICE HIMSELF.” — The Courage of Marine Corporal Jason Dunham.

On April 14, 2004, near the Syrian border in Husaybah, Iraq, 22-year-old Marine Corporal Jason Dunham was leading a rifle squad with 3rd Battalion, 7th Marines (3/7), moving to relieve a battalion commander’s convoy that had been ambushed.

After intercepting a line of suspicious vehicles attempting to flee the area, Dunham moved in on foot to conduct a search:

 As Dunham approached, an insurgent leaped from one of the vehicles and attacked him. Dunham immediately engaged the fighter in violent hand-to-hand combat to subdue him.

During the wrestling match on the dirt road, the insurgent pulled the pin on a hand grenade and dropped it between them.

Spotting two of his Marines—Lance Corporal William Hampton and PFC Kelly Miller—rushing in to assist him, Dunham shouted a warning: “No, no, watch out!” Without hesitation, he unstrapped his Kevlar helmet, slammed it over the grenade, and threw his entire body on top, pressing down with both hands to smother the blast.

The grenade exploded, shredding the helmet and mortally wounding Dunham. But his body and helmet absorbed the overwhelming force of the blast, saving both of his fellow Marines from fatal shrapnel.

Corporal Dunham was evacuated and succumbed to his wounds eight days later on April 22, 2004, at Bethesda Naval Hospital with his parents at his bedside.

On January 11, 2007, President George W. Bush presented the Medal of Honor posthumously to his family, making Jason Dunham the first Marine in the Iraq War to receive the nation’s highest military decoration. His legacy lives on across the fleet aboard the guided-missile destroyer USS Jason Dunham (DDG-109).

In an era where so few bear the burden of service, what does Corporal Jason Dunham’s split-second decision to smother a live grenade tell us about the heart of an American Marine?

“23 POUNDS OF STEEL. HUNDREDS OF ROUNDS OF 7.62. WELCOME TO THE JUNGLE.” — The Brutal Reality of Humping “The Pig” in Vietnam.

In the dense, suffocating heat of the Vietnamese jungle, infantrymen gave the M60 machine gun a nickname that stuck for generations: “The Pig.”

It earned the name honestly—because of its bulky, cumbersome weight, ferocious appetite for belted ammunition, and bone-jarring recoil when ripping through the brush:

• The Physical Punishment: At 23.15 pounds unloaded, the M60 was already a beast to carry. Factor in a spare barrel, an asbestos heat mitt, cleaning kit, and 500 to 1,000 rounds of linked 7.62×51mm NATO ammunition draped in crisscrossed bandoliers across the gunner and assistant gunner's chests, and a gun team was humping 70+ pounds through chest-high, razor-sharp elephant grass and knee-deep mud in 100-degree humidity.

• The Squad’s Lifeline: Firing at a sustained 550 to 650 rounds per minute with an effective range of over 1,100 meters, the M60 was the squad's primary base of fire. When an infantry patrol walked into an L-shaped ambush in the triple canopy, the distinctive heavy thumping roar of "The Pig" chewing through tree trunks was the only thing that bought troops time to maneuver.

• The Quirks: Early models lacked a carrying handle on the barrel, forcing gunners to use a bulky asbestos mitt to swap out glowing-red barrels mid-firefight. It was prone to jamming in red clay dust and mud, but when properly cleaned and fed, it delivered unmatched stopping power.

To the veterans who carried or fought alongside "The Pig" in Vietnam, the Gulf, or beyond: did you love it for its devastating firepower, or curse it every time you had to hump it up a ridgeline?

Todd is my hero every single day. Today, his Recon #Marine Brothers are the true heroes of the story. Thank you will never be enough 😭🇺🇸😭

But Todd has gained even more over these past 6 years. He's shown the world that you don't need feet to leave footprints on people's hearts. Eric Byron Shaw

DATE OF BIRTH: June 23, 1979
PLACE OF BIRTH: Attleboro, Massachusetts
HOME OF RECORD: Exeter, Maine

AWARDS BY DATE OF ACTION: Distinguished Service Cross
AWARDED FOR ACTIONS
DURING Global War on Terror
Service: Army
Battalion: 2d Battalion
Division: 101st Airborne Division (Air Assault)

GENERAL ORDERS:
Department of the Army, General Orders No. 73 (October 22, 2013)

CITATION:
The President of the United States of America, authorized by Act of Congress July 9, 1918, takes pride in presenting the Distinguished Service Cross (Posthumously) to Staff Sergeant Eric B. Shaw, United States Army, for extraordinary heroism in connection with military operations against an armed enemy while serving as a Squad Leader with Company C, 2d Battalion, 327th Infantry Regiment, 1st Brigade Combat Team, 101st Airborne Division (Air Assault) during combat operations against an armed enemy in Marawara District, Kunar Province, Afghanistan from 27 June 2010 to 28 June 2010. As Staff Sergeant Shaw's squad was attempting to seize the village of Daridam, he realized that a platoon of their Afghan Army partners were cut off from the squad and exposed to effective enemy fire. With complete disregard for his own safety, Staff Sergeant Shaw immediately rushed to their aid and rallied the soldiers. While successfully leading the soldiers out of imminent danger to rejoin United States forces, Staff Sergeant Shaw was felled by enemy fire. His bravery and selflessness saved the lives of twelve Afghan soldiers and enabled the forces to consolidate, continue fighting and accomplish their mission. Staff Sergeant Shaw's courage and self sacrifice at the cost of his own life, in order to save the lives of others is the epitome of valorous military service. Staff Sergeant Shaw's actions are in keeping with the finest traditions of military service and reflect great credit upon himself, Company C, 2d Battalion, 327th Infantry Regiment, 1st Brigade Combat Team, 101st Airborne Division (Air Assault) and the United States Army.

#Marines, Staff Sgt. Juan Rodrigues-Chavez (left) and Capt. Adeomola Fabayo received the Navy Cross at the National Museum of the Marine Corps on June 10, 2011, for their heroic actions in Afghanistan's Kunar Province in September 2009.

June 12, 2011 -- For two Marines attached to Marine Embedded Training Team 2-8, Regional Corps Advisory Command 3-7, in Kunar Province, Afghanistan, the morning of Sept. 8, 2009 started simple enough.

Then the world exploded around them.

Their actions during the ensuing fight earned them the nation’s second-highest award for valor. Secretary of the Navy Ray Mabus presented Capt. Ademola D. Fabayo and Staff Sgt. Juan J. Rodriguez-Chavez with the Navy Cross during a ceremony at the National Museum of the Marine Corps on June 10.

On that fateful day, then 1st Lt. Fabayo was leading a dismounted patrol of Americans and two platoons of Afghan National Security Forces into Ganjgal Village for a pre-dawn meeting with village elders. A short distance away, Rodriguez-Chavez was part of the team’s security element, ready to help his teammates if necessary.

The team was attacked by more than 50 enemy fighters, who rained down machine gun fire and rocket-propelled grenades from fortified positions. Four members of the team were cut off and exposed to the murderous fire.

With no regard for his own life, Fabayo pushed forward on foot into the kill zone in an attempt to regain contact, effectively engaging the enemy at close range with his M4 rifle. When a U.S. Army advisor was severely wounded, Fabayo moved from a covered position under heavy fire to assist in his recovery, helping carry him across several hundred meters of fire-swept ground.

He then gotten into an unarmored truck with another advisor and pushed back into the kill zone, ignoring the rounds striking the truck, as they attempted to rescue the fallen members of their team.

While Fabayo was attacking, Rodriguez-Chavez wasted no time getting into the fight as well. With members of his team in immediate danger, he drove a gun truck, with one other Marine as his gunner, forward into the kill zone of the ambush with only the machine gun fire of his gunner to suppress the enemy. He repeatedly ignored the heavy enemy fire and drove the vehicle into the kill zone three times to cover the withdrawal of the force and evacuate two dozen members of the Afghan National Security Forces.

The two Marines, along with two other members of their team, then consolidated their force into an armored Humvee, Rodriguez-Chavez at the wheel and Fabayo in the gunners turret, manning the machine gun. They made yet another extremely hazardous trip into the deepest point of the kill zone, where Rodriguez-Chavez positioned his vehicle to shield his teammates from the intense enemy fire as they dismounted to recover the fallen warriors.

During the ceremony, Mabus said that the Marines repeatedly exposed themselves to enemy fire and demonstrated the kind of valor that should be taught to every Marine in boot camp.

Captain Kent Solheim, United States Army, was awarded the Silver Star for actions during a raid in Karbala, Iraq, where he courageously saved multiple American lives by disregarding his personal safety.

On July 27, 2007, Captain Kent Solheim, United States Army, participated in Operation VOLCANO II, an operation designed to capture a senior leader of the infamous Shiite militia, the Mahdi Army, in the city of Karbala, Iraq. Solheim's team "fast roped" from helicopters into the area and set up their position near the target building. Insurgents viciously attacked the American forces from three sides with rocketpropelled grenades (RPGs) and AK-47s. As the enemy fire got heavier, combat air support was called in to eliminate some of the aggressors, but a significant number of attackers remained to the north of Solheim and his unit. These insurgents used the dust that the assault force's helicopters had kicked up to conceal their movements.
With the insurgents targeting one of the American positions, Solheim aggressively maneuvered his men to reinforce the beleaguered soldiers. It was then that he noticed an insurgent armed with an RPG, less than ten meters away from his position. Disregarding any concern for himself, he bravely charged forward, shot and killed the insurgent, saving the Americans in the nick of time. Realizing that the US forces in the building were in grave danger, Solheim exposed himself to enemy fire in order to gain a better position to cover the other soldiers in his unit. From this location, he managed to limit the insurgent fire on his team. In the final moments of the engagement, he rounded a corner and he found himself face to face with an AK-47-wielding Mahdi fighter. Solheim made a split-second decision, firing at and killing the insurgent. However, as the terrorist fell to the ground fatally wounded, he let loose one last burst from his AK-47, which wounded Solheim in the legs and back.

Marine Lance Cpl. Brady Gustafson was manning a gun turret in an armored vehicle in Afghanistan when chaos struck. His squad was ambushed from multiple positions by enemy insurgents wielding rocket-propelled grenades and machine guns, including an RPG that burst through the hull of his vehicle and delivered a devastating injury to his right leg.

Gustafson refused to back down, however. Bleeding profusely, he engaged numerous enemy fighters while a Navy corpsman inside the vehicle cranked a tourniquet onto Gustfason’s leg. The hundreds of rounds of gunfire he delivered allowed Marines to evacuate another vehicle after it had burst into flames. The RPG blast knocked the Marine driving Gustafson’s vehicle unconscious, but Gustafson shouted at him until he woke up to push the burning Marine vehicle behind them out of the kill zone.

With the U.S. war in Iraq over and combat operations in Afghanistan winding down, Gustafson is now part of a select group of U.S. troops who didn’t receive the Medal of Honor but who have advocates who say they should. In Gustafson’s case, that includes his former battalion commander, Col. Richard Hall, who says he regrets not nominating him for the higher award. Gustafson was put in for the Silver Star, the nation’s third-highest award for combat valor, and ultimately received the Navy Cross. He left the service as a corporal in 2009.

“THEY PULLED MY TWO BOYS OUT AT GUNPOINT IN THEIR UNDERWEAR.” — Navy SEAL Chief Eddie Gallagher on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the foundational episodes in the history of The Shawn Ryan Show (Episode #008), decorated Special Warfare Operator Chief (SOC) Eddie Gallagher detailed the dawn raid on his family home by heavily armed federal agents.

In his own words:

“I had just returned from my eighth combat deployment. I was undergoing medical treatment at the base hospital for traumatic brain injury when NCIS showed up at our front door at sunrise.

They didn't knock. They pulled up in tactical vehicles with assault rifles drawn, wearing full battle rattle like they were raiding an Al-Qaeda compound in Fallujah.

My wife and our two young sons were asleep inside. The agents stormed into the bedrooms, ripped the blankets off my boys, and dragged them out onto the street in their underwear at gunpoint.

Neighbors were coming out of their homes watching my terrified kids standing on the sidewalk with laser sights pointed at their chests while agents searched our house.

They threw me into handcuffs, drove me to the brig, and tossed me into solitary confinement alongside convicted rapists and murderers before I had even been charged with a single crime. That’s when I realized the battle wasn’t in Iraq anymore—the enemy was right inside our own government.”

After enduring months in pretrial solitary confinement, Gallagher fought the charges in a historic military court-martial where the prosecution's case famously unraveled on the stand, resulting in his acquittal on all major murder and war-crime charges.

Pointing rifles and laser sights at the sleeping children of an active-duty combat veteran over allegations that collapsed in court remains one of the most controversial military justice actions in modern history.

Did military investigators cross an unforgivable line raiding a SEAL family's home like a terrorist hideout? Drop your take below.

Disclaimer: This content is published strictly for documentary, historical, and journalistic discussion, examining firsthand public commentary from combat veterans on the military justice system. It contains no depiction or endorsement of real-world violence or illegal activity.

Maj. John Caldwell, of the 85th Test and Evaluation Squadron, was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for his rapid airpower response to an enemy attack on American and allied forces during his deployment to Nuristan province, Afghanistan, May 2, 2011.

"The DFC is a unique group of individuals; you are about to enjoy elite company like Col. "Bud" Day [retired] who is here today," Col David W. Hicks, 53rd Wing commander and officiator, said to the F-16 pilot before he pinned on the honors.

The F-16 pilot, then rank of captain, responded to an ambush on a special operations team already taking casualties from effective fire. This timely attack allowed the assault team to momentarily regroup.
Hicks was deployed to the area at that time as well and experienced what it

was like to fly three to five hours a day hovering the war zone just in case of emergency.
"At those moments it seemed quiet, like nothing was going on," said the commander as a description of the sortie Air Force pilots perform covering military members on the ground. "But then in 10 to 20 minutes a decision has to be made resulting in life or death."

Caldwell quickly identified mortar flashes from the mountainside, rapidly derived coordinates and directed his wingman to employ a Joint Direct Attack Munition before refueling. According to the award narrative, he remained as the only kinetic asset protecting the assault force.

"I'd like to say I could take the credit, but it took a combined effort of military services to get the team on the ground out of the valley," said Caldwell.

From his F-16 cockpit, the pilot initiated coordination with the Combined Air Operations Center, conveyed the urgent need for medical evacuation and additional kinetic assets. He also contacted the separated assault team's command element, provided real time updates of the dire situation and gained approval to use any ordnance to protect them. Meanwhile, 90 insurgents began a flanking charge on the friendly position.

"Sadly, there were six American and coalition forces I couldn't help that day; they are the true heroes," said Caldwell. "I was at the right place at the right time and I believe anyone in my squadron would do the same thing."

His award citation said the pilot's life was at risk when he employed an immediate, nonstandard, danger close strafe run into the rugged, midnight black valley, breaking the inexorable charge as the enemy continued to fire with rounds impacting mere inches from the trapped allies. Caldwell immediately re-attacked with an expertly placed, danger close JDAM, completely neutralizing the ambush.

All that said, the pilot still would not call himself "hero."

"You don't get to define yourself as a 'hero,' others do," said Hicks. "Specifically, guys on the ground that night are telling the story of the F-16 that saved them and how they wouldn't be standing today, same goes for their families. The fact you did it speaks volumes on who you are as an aviator and what you did for our country."

The DFC narration said, according to the assault force commander, the presence of Caldwell and his immensely accurate awareness of the situation prevented a catastrophic loss of American lives and directly turned the tide of this engagement.

"Caldwell is not only an awesome fighter pilot, he also exemplifies our core value of 'service before self,'" said Lt. Col. Thomas Seymour, commander of the 85th Test and Evaluation Squadron, where Caldwell has served as weapons flight commander since January. "I think this medal is the result of his skill in the air and his willingness to put himself in harm's way in order to accomplish the mission."

In just a short time stationed here, the commander said the pilot won their group's Flight Commander of the Quarter award and fully embraced his new role as an operational test pilot.

Congress authorized The Distinguished Flying Cross, July 2, 1926, as an award for any military member of the U.S. who exhibited heroism or extraordinary achievement while participating in an aerial fight against an enemy of the U.S.

A FASCINATING MILITARY RANK SHOWDOWN

A compelling dynamic is unfolding in Washington as retired U.S. Navy Rear Admiral Nancy Lacore mounts a bid for Congress that could place her in a direct oversight role over Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

If elected to the House of Representatives, Admiral Lacore would become the highest-ranking female military officer ever to serve in the United States Congress.

In terms of military service, the rank difference is substantial. Hegseth served honorably as an Army National Guard Major (O-4), deploying to Iraq and Afghanistan. Lacore reached the rank of Two-Star Rear Admiral (O-8), serving decades as a naval aviator and flag officer.

While the Secretary of Defense holds ultimate civilian authority over the armed forces, having a retired Two-Star admiral on Capitol Hill creates a rare dynamic in congressional oversight of the Pentagon.

Does a higher military rank make someone a more qualified voice on defense policy, or does field-grade combat experience better represent the frontline warfighter?

June 28, 2005. The Hindu Kush mountains of Kunar Province, Afghanistan.

Deep behind enemy lines during Operation Red Wings, a 4-man Navy SEAL reconnaissance team—commanded by 29-year-old Lieutenant Michael P. Murphy—was ambushed on a sheer mountain ridgeline by over 50 Taliban fighters.

Outnumbered and taking fire from three sides, the four SEALs fought through a relentless, three-hour running gun battle. Every man was hit multiple times.

Trapped down in a ravine, the steep granite cliffs blocked all radio and satellite signals. Murphy knew with absolute certainty: without emergency close air support, none of his men were walking off that mountain alive.

Knowing it was almost certain death, Lieutenant Murphy made a leader's choice.

He deliberately walked out of cover onto an exposed, open rock ledge directly in the line of sight of dozens of enemy machine guns to get a satellite signal.

Calm under fire, Murphy dialed headquarters and relayed their exact coordinates: "My men are taking heavy fire... we're getting picked apart."

As he spoke, an enemy bullet punched through his back. He dropped the phone, picked it back up, finished the transmission, and signed off with words that will live forever in military history:

"Thank you, sir."

Mortally wounded, Murphy crawled back to his fighting position and continued returning fire alongside his men until his last breath.

His final transmission allowed the rescue force to scramble, ultimately saving the life of Marcus Luttrell.

In 2007, Lieutenant Michael P. Murphy was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor—the first service member to receive the nation’s highest award for valor in the War in Afghanistan.

A leader never asks his men to do what he isn't willing to do himself.

A MARITIME STANDOFF AT AMERICAN PORTS

As a naval aviator who served nearly a decade on active duty flying missions throughout Europe and the Middle East, Sherrill framed the decision as a straightforward matter of national security and international accountability.

“SHOULD TAXPAYER WELFARE CASH BE RESTRICTED TO BASIC SURVIVAL NEEDS?” — Florida has become the first state in the country to implement strict new regulations blocking public assistance cash benefits from being spent on tattoos, vaping products, theme park admissions, and other luxury services as part of a statewide crackdown on welfare fraud and waste.

“We think that will ultimately save taxpayer money and reduce fraud, but also will help our efforts to get folks the true help that they need. At its core, this is about responsible stewardship and making sure taxpayer resources support family stability and self-sufficiency, not luxury purchases.”

— Florida Governor Ron DeSantis

Key Elements of Florida's Welfare Reform
First-in-the-Nation TANF Amendment: Florida officially amended its Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) State Plan to establish explicit point-of-sale and ATM withdrawal bans for non-essential purchases on state-issued Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) cards.

Prohibited Business & Service Categories: The updated restrictions bar cash-assistance benefits from being spent at tattoo and piercing studios, vape and tobacco shops, theme parks and entertainment attractions, casinos and gaming parlors, tanning salons, adult entertainment venues, and luxury spas.

Focusing on Essential Family Needs: Administered through the Florida Department of Children and Families, the measure mandates that cash welfare benefits be directed exclusively toward essential living costs—including food, housing, utilities, child clothing, and job-training expenses.

Potential National Blueprint: The policy establishes a precedent currently being evaluated by federal lawmakers and multiple other state legislatures seeking to tighten public assistance spending rules nationwide.

The Public Debate
Arguments in Favor: Supporters emphasize that public assistance programs exist as temporary safety nets funded by hardworking taxpayers. Restricting non-essential spending protects program integrity, deters benefit trafficking, and ensures public funds directly aid struggling children and families.

Arguments in Opposition: Critics contend that TANF cash stipends are already very limited (averaging around $300 per month for a family of three in Florida) with strict work requirements, arguing that new merchant-category prohibitions create additional administrative friction and unfairly stigmatize assistance recipients.

A veteran who survived roadside bombs and combat deployments shouldn’t lose their life in a civilian hospital or VA clinic because a corporate claims adjuster denied a pre-authorization.

Every single week, we hear the same story:

A doctor prescribes a critical scan, a specialized surgery, or a life-saving medication.

“PARATROOPERS DON’T CLOCK OUT: HEARD GUNSHOTS & RAN DOWNSTAIRS WITH IMPROVISED MEDICAL GEAR.”

Paratroopers don't clock out. When gunfire erupted outside his apartment building, Sergeant Brian Lieberman didn't lock his door and wait for the police. He ran straight into the courtyard, found a victim with an open chest wound, and built an airtight chest seal with plastic wrap and tape to keep her lungs from collapsing.

On June 5, 2023, then-Specialist Brian R. Lieberman—a combat medic with the 1st Brigade Combat Team, 82nd Airborne Division—was off-duty at his apartment complex in Fayetteville, North Carolina, when rapid gunfire shattered the evening quiet.

Without body armor or advanced medical equipment, he grabbed his legally owned firearm and sprinted downstairs toward the active shooter:

Sprinting to the Fire: Arriving in the courtyard, Lieberman identified himself as an Army combat medic and located a female victim suffering from a critical penetrating sucking chest wound.

Shielding Under Secondary Fire: As he began treating her, the active shooter circled back in a vehicle and opened fire directly at them. Lieberman threw his body across the wounded woman to act as a human shield, drew his sidearm, returned fire, and drove the shooter away.

The Improvised Chest Seal: With air and blood entering her chest cavity and no standard trauma kit on hand, Lieberman improvised an occlusive chest seal using a plastic bag and tape, venting trapped air to prevent a fatal tension pneumothorax.

Fighting Traumatic Shock: He treated the victim for hypovolemic shock and kept her conscious until Fayetteville Police and EMS arrived, saving her life.

For his valor and composure, Colonel Jason Schuerger presented Sergeant Lieberman with the Soldier's Medal—the U.S. Army's highest non-combat award for heroism. In October 2026, he was formally recognized as an Angel of the Battlefield recipient.

“Without a doubt our Airborne medics move to the sound of gunfire to save lives,” said Col. Schuerger. “Of course he moved to the sound of gunfire, of course he administered aid, of course he saved somebody's life.”

Lieberman’s guidance to fellow medics reflects the heart of the Airborne:

“I always tell my junior medics to never lose their passion for the craft of medicine. That way no matter where they are, no matter what they're doing, they can always be there for someone on their worst day.”

All American valor in action.

The U.S. military has always been fertile soil for firsts throughout our nation’s history, and the promotion of Carol A. Mutter to become the nation’s first female lieutenant general serves as a perfect case in point for Women’s History Month.

Women have served in the military from the earliest years of our representative republic.

Deborah Sampson (Gannett) served covertly when she disguised herself as a man under the assumed name of Robert Shurtleff, to join the Continental Army and fight in the Revolutionary War in 1782. Sampson went so far as to cut a musket ball out of her own thigh to prevent a battlefield surgeon from discovering her true gender. She was honorably discharged as a private in 1793.

Women gained the opportunity to serve openly in World War 1 when Congress opened the military to women in 1914. However, it took more than two centuries between the time Sampson first shouldered a musket to the time when women served as general (flag rank) officers in the American military. Mutter achieved one-star brigadier general rank in 1991.

Three years later Mutter became the first woman in the history of America’s military to achieve two-star major general rank in 1994, and two years after that in 1996 she became the first woman to become a three-star lieutenant general in any American military branch.

Born in 1945 in Greeley, Colorado, Mutter graduated in 1967 from officer candidate school at the University of Northern Colorado as a second lieutenant in the Marine Corps.

Mutter had a number of firsts during her 32-year career in the Corps:

•First woman to qualify as Command Center Crew Commander/Space Director at U.S. Space Command.
• First woman of flag rank (general officer rank) to command a major deployable tactical command.
• First woman Marine major general, and senior woman in all the services at that time.
• First woman nominated by a U.S. president (Bill Clinton) for three-star rank.
• First female lieutenant general in the U.S. Armed Forces.

During a 2014 interview for the documentary Unsung Heroes: The Story of America's Female Patriots, Mutter explains why she joined the Marine Corps during the early years of the Vietnam War.

“Because they're the best, there's no doubt about that,” she said. “ ... when I joined, (the Corps) was only one percent female and there were no women in the deployed forces at all. So, as long as the women were back in the rear doing the jobs that the men didn't want to do, there was not much of a problem.”

The general has been recognized as a trailblazer by several different organizations. Among them is the National Women’s Hall of Fame, which inducted the general in 2017.

Mutter retired from the Corps in 1999 and lives with her husband at their home in Lookout Mountain, Tennessee.

SSG Jamyn Peterson wouldn't describe himself as a hero, he said. However, during his last deployment to the remote Oruzgan province in Afghanistan from December 2006 until January 2008, the Army Reservist repeatedly demonstrated his dedication to his comrades and to his duties. Peterson was recognized for his service with a Purple Heart and two Bronze Star Medals, one with ‘Valor.'

The second Bronze Star recognized his performance as team leader as “absolutely phenomenal,” according to the award citation. But it was the bravery he demonstrated during an ambush that earned him the Bronze Star with ‘Valor.”

“I was honored,” Peterson said of receiving the medal, “but I was more honored that my guys got them.”

SSG Matt Winters and SGT Ben Mogenson were riding with him on June 16, 2007 when their convoy was ambushed on the road home. When a bomb exploded just feet from their truck, the truck leading the convoy sped ahead to avoid the blast. But they took a wrong turn.

Peterson and his team had a choice: stay on the road that led back to camp or follow their comrades the wrong way into enemy territory. They decided to follow their comrades.

It wasn't long before the first truck was hit by a rocket propelled grenade that went right through it, forcing everyone out of the truck. And while there were
only six soldiers between their two trucks, “there were over 100 bad guys. They were only 90 feet away. You could see them. They were just lined up,” he said.
“It was like hail coming down on the truck. It was like incessant bullets raining,” Peterson said. That's when he directed his vehicle right into the middle of the ambush to provide cover and support to the disabled vehicle.

“The one thing I remember was that I could have stayed in the truck and gotten killed, but if I got out of the truck I was going to get killed. Pretty much we were going to die,” he said. “Life flashes before you.”

But Peterson did get out of the truck, and was able to set up behind the hood of the disabled vehicle so he could provide cover while the other soldiers tended to the injured. They were able to hold the enemy at bay until Afghan Army soldiers arrived on the scene to help. When the enemy saw the two trucks with 15 Afghan soldiers in it, they started to flee, Peterson said.

“They kind of saved our lives,” Peterson said. “We'd built enough of a rapport,” he said, “that they came to help us.” It was an act which demonstrated not only their loyalty, but also their bravery, he said.

Peterson spoke as highly of Winters and Mogenson.

“They were more aware of what was going on. That's more brave than me,” he said. “Those guys were aware what was going on and still kept at it. They did a great job.”

Peterson, however, said he is most proud of his work with the people of the Oruzgan province. Working with the local community, he and his team set up the only local health clinic for miles around, a radio station, as well as a primary school for the local children that teaches reading, writing, arithmetic and Islam.

“Any good we wanted to do, we were able to do it,” Peterson said. “Being out in the middle of nowhere, I thought I was in a place where I belonged.”

Despite the enemy's opposition to the school, the students would get up at five in the morning to walk five miles to school. They would have to skirt Taliban checkpoints to avoid getting beaten, Peterson said.

“They are worried if they're going to get beaten with sticks on the way to school, and they'd still come,” Peterson said. The enemy “rocketed us twice while the students were in there, but they kept coming.”

“It was a pretty amazing experience. A good learning experience,” he said of the deployment. “That's one thing that I take away from this, how the human being can adapt to any situation.”

Peterson is still an active reservist training troops heading to Afghanistan.

“That's what I have a passion for now, making sure that these troops are ready to hit the ground when they go down range,” he said.

Peterson, who will likely redeploy shortly, said it's important to remember that the army is made up of individual men and women.

“If I don't go, someone less experienced will have to go. There's an obligation there,” he said. “Somebody's got to do it.”

Sergeant Matthew Abbate sprinted around in a live minefield, breaking an enemy ambush, clearing a landing zone, and evacuating critically wounded casualties.

Sgt Abbate, a Scout Sniper from 3rd Battalion, 5th Marines, patrolled with his squad through Sangin, Afghanistan on October 14, 2010. Taliban fighters opened up on the Marines from multiple positions. The patrol leader fell. The rest of the squad scattered for cover. As they spread out, two Marines and the patrol Corpsman suddenly stepped on anti-personnel mines, knocking them down one by one in rapid succession. The Marines were unaware they had entered a live minefield. Still under fire, Abbate ignored the danger and sprinted through the area, directing the remaining Marines onto targets and suppressing the enemy with his own weapon. The Taliban broke contact in the face of the Marines' accurate fire.

Abbate called for emergency medevac for the wounded, then swept the area for remaining explosives that could prevent a chopper from landing. While he cleared the LZ, the Taliban resumed their attack. Abbate again ran through the minefield, took charge of the remaining Marines, and led them in a counter-attack. The Taliban broke off once more, and Abbate called in the LZ secure for evacuation.

Former U.S. Army Ranger Sergeant Nicholas Irving, known across the special operations community as "The Reaper," became one of the most lethal snipers in Ranger history during a single deployment to Afghanistan in 2009 (Wikipedia).

Serving with the 3rd Ranger Battalion of the 75th Ranger Regiment—and becoming the first African American sniper in his battalion—Irving was credited with 33 kills over roughly 100 days with his SR-25 rifle, "Dirty Diana" (Wikipedia).

Originally hoping to become a Navy SEAL before a colorblindness test redirected him to the Army Rangers, Irving completed three tours in Iraq and one in Afghanistan before retiring from active duty in 2010 and sharing his story in the bestselling memoir The Reaper

Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd announced the retirement of heroic police dog K9 Ace, who saved the lives of three deputies during a shootout in Kathleen, Florida (FOX 13 Tampa Bay).

While deputies were serving a felony warrant, an armed suspect opened fire in the woods. K9 Ace charged forward and took gunfire meant for the deputies, allowing the team to eliminate the threat without deputy casualties (WFLA News Channel 8).

Ace underwent emergency life-saving surgery that required amputating his front leg. Despite losing a limb, the resilient 7-year-old canine walked into Sheriff Judd's office on three legs with his tail wagging, earning an official retirement salute after six years of dedicated law enforcement service (Polk County Sheriff's Office).
